transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 57 mins
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, Sageleaf), Diego Morales (Lead ML Eng), Maya Patel (Product), Evan Li (Infra), Olivia Park (Dev)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro — I'm Lena, AE on the account, and Marcus will walk through the SDK and auth patterns. Could each of you say a short hello?
[00:10] Aisha Khan: Hi, this is Aisha — CTO at Sageleaf, thanks for doing this. We're focused on getting our prototypes onto a stable inference stack.
[00:16] Diego Morales: Diego here, lead ML infra. Main interest is minimal friction for devs and reasonable latency/cost tradeoffs.
[00:22] Marcus Chen: Great — we'll aim to show both Python and TypeScript flows, how the environment variables should be set, and a Console-centric dev loop if you prefer that.
[00:30] Lena Park: Also plan to cover Redwood Optimize suggestions and how batching/kv cache impacts unit cost.
[00:36] Maya Patel: Quick ask from product — we want to see how the console ties into monitoring, e.g., token cost per route.
[00:42] Evan Li: From infra, we need to confirm SSO for Console and whether we can do VPC/private deployment later.

[03:05] Marcus Chen: Okay jumping into the demo. First, pip install redwood-sdk, and npm install @redwood/inference for TypeScript. For Python the basic pattern is: set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, then from redwood import RedwoodClient, client = RedwoodClient()...
[03:35] Olivia Park: Small nit — is the package name the same in PyPI and the npm registry? We have a CI check that pins names.
[03:41] Marcus Chen: Good call. PyPI name is redwood-inference-client, npm package is @redwood/inference. We'll include exact pinned versions in the follow-up email.

[06:10] Marcus Chen: Auth patterns: for quickstarts we recommend API key stored in env vars for local dev. Example .env:
REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx
REDWOOD_ENV=prod\/dev (optional)
REDWOOD_REGION=us-west-2 (if using hosted region routing)
Also we support direct SSO into the Console — that is SAML or OIDC for enterprise users.
[06:45] Diego Morales: If we do Private deployment, does auth still go through Redwood control plane? We prefer to keep auth inside our VPC if possible.
[06:53] Lena Park: For Private you can run the control plane on customer-managed network; API tokens are still the recommended short-term approach, but we do have integrations for KMS-backed secrets and your SSO so you can manage access internally. We'll detail that.

[09:20] Marcus Chen: Walkthrough Python quickstart: show sample code for text generation, streaming helper, and handling retries. (Marcus shares screen, code pasted.)
[09:45] Marcus Chen (screen): from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate(model='rw-1-large', prompt='Summarize this email...')
print(resp.text)

[11:00] Olivia Park: Are there official wrappers for streaming in Python? We want event-based processing in our pipeline.
[11:08] Marcus Chen: Yes — there is a stream() helper that yields tokens; you can attach processors. Note: streaming stability depends on connection and region, but it's robust.

[13:15] Marcus Chen: TS example: import {Redwood} from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.generate({ model: 'rw-1-large', prompt: '...' });
[13:35] Maya Patel: For product, how quickly can non-engineers try the Console? We want PMs to poke at outputs without running code.
[13:42] Lena Park: Console has a quickstart playground tied to your API key and you can create routes, pin model versions, and view token cost per route. We'll show a short Console demo next.

[16:00] Marcus Chen: Switching to Console: show project creation, environment variables UI, and route creation. Note the 'sandbox' toggle for safe testing that doesn't incur quota.
[16:28] Marcus Chen (screen): Here is the Routes view — per-route token metrics, latency percentiles, and the Optimize suggestions tab.
[17:05] Aisha Khan: How opinionated are Optimize suggestions? Our prompts are fairly long, and we don't want aggressive quantization suggestions that hurt quality.
[17:14] Marcus Chen: Optimize runs workload analysis and suggests batching, cache prefix rules, and quantization profiles with expected delta in quality and cost. All suggestions are actionable toggles and labeled with expected token-cost delta and latency impact. You can also pin "safety-first" settings that disallow quantization beyond some threshold.

[20:00] Diego Morales: Could you show an example of prefix caching? We have chat-style flows with repeated system instructions.
[20:08] Marcus Chen: Sure — prefix caching example: mark system prompt as cacheable and it stores KV cache for subsequent calls with same prefix. This reduces token compute and latency. Caveat: it's only available for models and runtimes that preserve KV cache across sessions; we'll include a compatibility matrix in follow-up.

[23:30] Lena Park: Security questions — SOC 2, encryption-at-rest/in-transit, audit logs, and KMS integrations are key asks. We have a SOC 2 report and KMS patterns; Marcus will attach the docs.
[23:55] Marcus Chen: Quick note on audit logs: Console exports request-level logs to your configured S3 or syslog for Private deployments; for Hosted we retain logs per policy and can stream to your SIEM.

[26:40] Evan Li: For SSO/SAML, is role-based access supported? We don't want blanket admin access.
[26:48] Marcus Chen: Absolutely — Console supports RBAC with SCIM for user provisioning and you can map groups to role sets (viewer, developer, admin). We'll share the SSO metadata endpoint and sample SAML XML in the doc bundle.

[30:00] Marcus Chen: Back to SDK: environment patterns for CI — we recommend ephemeral credentials for CI jobs. For long-running services, use Redwood token manager and rotate keys every 30 days. Also, put service-level keys in your secret manager and reference via env var in container spec.
[30:28] Olivia Park: Our CI uses GitHub Actions; any starter action?
[30:35] Marcus Chen: We'll include a GitHub Actions snippet that injects secrets into the job; simple pattern with REDWOOD_API_KEY as secret.

[33:10] Diego Morales: On the model side, we need latency budgets: 95th < 500ms for small prompts. Does Redwood have dedicated capacity for that SLA?
[33:20] Lena Park: Yes, Redwood Dedicated offers committed GPU pools and you can set target latency SLOs. For pilot we often start on Hosted and move to Dedicated if throughput latency variance matters.

[35:40] Marcus Chen: A quick detour into quantization: we support int8 and 4-bit paths depending on model. Optimize will suggest quantization only when historical evals indicate acceptable quality delta. For safety you can opt out per-model.
[36:05] Maya Patel: Do you run internal evals or do we provide eval prompts?
[36:12] Marcus Chen: Both. We run initial evals and recommend you supply your prompt sets for regression testing; the Console links regression alerts to prompt suites.

[38:50] Marcus Chen: I'm going to demo a small local benchmark script — simple loop that calls client.generate with your prompt set and measures p50/p95 latency and token cost. (Runs sample results, screen shows CSV output)
[40:10] Diego Morales: Seems straightforward. For our POC, we'd want that script to produce a heatmap by prompt length. Can you parameterize that?
[40:22] Marcus Chen: Yes, we can add length buckets and export JSON. I'll include the modified script in the follow-up.

[42:30] Lena Park: Procurement note — you asked about contract terms and data residency earlier. For US customers we offer hosted in us-west/us-east; dedicated and private provide stronger residency controls. I'll have legal join next call if you want to see draft terms.
[42:48] Aisha Khan: Yes please. Also can you confirm log retention windows for hosted? We need 90-day retention for some telemetry.
[42:56] Marcus Chen: Hosted default is 30 days, can be extended as an add-on to 90+ days. Private gives you full control.

[45:10] Olivia Park: Small thing — error codes we would see on rate limiting vs model capacity? We want to programmatic fallback handling.
[45:18] Marcus Chen: There are distinct HTTP codes: 429 for rate limiting, 503 for capacity fallbacks, and structured error body with retry-after and suggested fallback model id. There's also a client-level retry helper.

[48:00] Marcus Chen: Quick note on SDK versioning — we version the SDKs per major release; breaking changes are called out in the changelog and Console warns about pinned route model mismatches.

[50:00] Lena Park: Recap and next steps. We'll send: code snippets (Python/TS), a Console screencast, SOC2 and SSO config docs, and a benchmark script. Marcus, anything to add?
[50:12] Marcus Chen: I'll prepare the benchmark and tweak it for Sageleaf's prompt set. Also I'll include a compatibility matrix for caching and quantization.

[52:00] Aisha Khan: Timeline — we'd like to kick a short pilot next week and lock infra details in the scoping call. Can we aim to start Aug 25 for a 2-week pilot?
[52:10] Lena Park: Yes, we'll schedule the scoping call for Aug 21 to finalize infra and success criteria, then start the pilot on Aug 25.

[54:30] Maya Patel: Final product question — does the Console let us annotate bad model outputs and feed them back to an eval?
[54:38] Marcus Chen: Yes, Console has a feedback loop — you can flag outputs, tie them to a prompt suite, and set alert thresholds for regressions.

[56:00] Lena Park: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and lock the August scoping slot.
[56:09] Aisha Khan: Thanks all.

[56:20] (call ends)
notes: Follow-up email will include pinned SDK versions and sample .env
